## Data

Load the pocessed participant data as returned from the script 'code/sma_dataprocessing.R'. Note, the current script depends on you running the sma_dataprocessing.R script prior in order to access the returned data object. This is to reduce computational demands and redundancies.

```{r}
#| label: data-import
#| cache: false

data <- readRDS(here::here("data", "experiment1", "processed", "data.RDS"))
data_params <- readRDS(here::here("data", "experiment1", "modelling", "parameters", "m3_para_data.RDS"))
```

```{r}
# display summary statistics of model parameters
cat("Model parameter summary statistics:\n")

summary_stats <- data_params |>
  dplyr::select(a_tiktok, a_netflix, 
                strap_tiktok_avg, strap_netflix_avg, 
                wl_tiktok, wl_netflix) |>
  summary()

print(summary_stats)
```

For computational reasons, we will perform analyses on the raw scores of wanting and liking estimates for both conditions. Whereas the z-transformation helps with interpretation purposes, the standardisation causes problems with later analyses which perform standardisation as part of the statistical test. Specicially, the Bayesfactor package works with standardised effect sizes, meaning performing the analyses on the z-transformed data results in a double-transformation.

```{r}
#| label: z-transformation

# get the mean and standard deviation for wanting estimates (across conditions)
a_mean <- mean(c(data_params$a_netflix, data_params$a_tiktok), na.rm = TRUE)
a_sd <- sd(c(data_params$a_netflix, data_params$a_tiktok), na.rm = TRUE)

# get the mean and standard deviation for liking estimates (across conditions)
strap_mean <- mean(c(data_params$strap_netflix_avg, data_params$strap_tiktok_avg), na.rm = TRUE)
strap_sd <- sd(c(data_params$strap_netflix_avg, data_params$strap_tiktok_avg), na.rm = TRUE)

# z-transform variables
data_params <- data_params |>
  mutate(
    # wanting estimates
    a_netflix_z = (a_netflix - a_mean) / a_sd,
    a_tiktok_z = (a_tiktok - a_mean) / a_sd,
    
    # liking estimates
    strap_netflix_avg_z = (strap_netflix_avg - strap_mean) / strap_sd,
    strap_tiktok_avg_z = (strap_tiktok_avg - strap_mean) / strap_sd,
    
    # wanting liking difference
    wl_tiktok_z = a_tiktok_z - strap_tiktok_avg_z,
    wl_netflix_z = a_netflix_z - strap_netflix_avg_z
  )
```

## Compliance

The experimental procedure involved several compliance questions that were included to assess participants' adherence to the protocol. Participants who indicated that they had not complied to either the task or the waiting period part of the experiment were given the opportunity to provide an open response explanation. We used all available information to asses participants' compliance.

To examine the effect of this and other decisions, we report the effects on our findings in 'sma_sensitivity.qmd'. Specifically, we provide sensitivity analyses for a) analyses on the entire sample, and b) analyses on the sample that excludes anyone who indicated that they had not complied to some aspect of the experimental procedure (regardless of explanations).

### Task compliance

Compliance to the task instructions was assessed asking participants to indicate whether they had used the same finger to press the mouse throughout the task, with binary Yes/No response options.

```{r}
#| label: compliance-reasons

data_params |> dplyr::filter(task_tiktok_compliance_text != "NA") |> pull(task_tiktok_compliance_text)
data_params |> dplyr::filter(task_netflix_compliance_text != "NA") |> pull(task_netflix_compliance_text)
```

The reasons for task non-compliance included a) accidental switching of the fingers used to click, or b) deliberate but brief changes in finger use. We consider both of these 'violations' to be minor and do not exclude participants who accidentally or briefly switched fingers throughout the effort expenditure task.

### Waiting compliance

Compliance to the instructions of the waiting period was assessed using the question 'Did you use \[TikTok/Netflix\] for the entire duration of the waiting period', with binary Yes/No response options.

```{r}
#| label: compliance-reasons-watching
#| warning: false
#| cache: false

# non-compliance during TikTok condition
data_params |> dplyr::filter(watch_tiktok_compliance_text != "NA") |> pull(watch_tiktok_compliance_text)

# non-compliance during Netflix condition
data_params |> dplyr::filter(watch_netflix_compliance_text != "NA") |> pull(watch_netflix_compliance_text)
```

The reasons for waiting period non-compliance included 1) internet problems, 2) engaging in other activities, or 3) continuing to watch Netflix from where one had left off before. We consider internet problems (1) and engaging in other activities (2) to be non-compliance that may affect the validity of the results. Therefore, the following analyses exclude participants who indicated this.

```{r}
#| label: compliance-exclusion
#| cache: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| include: false

# get subject identifier of participant reading magazines
p_excl <- data_params |> 
  dplyr::filter(watch_netflix_compliance_text == "I also go through the magazines briefly") |> 
  pull(subj_id)

# exclude participants based on compliance violations
data_params <- data_params |>
  dplyr::filter(watch_tiktok_compliance == TRUE) |> # exclude TikTok non-compliers
  dplyr::filter(subj_id != p_excl) # exclude Netflix non-compliers
```

Following the above exclusions based on non-compliance during the task or waiting period of the experiment, we continue with the analyses based on a sample of **`r sprintf("%.0f", nrow(data_params))`** participants.

### Session Timing and Duration

Get the average number of days between the first and second session of participants.

```{r}
#| label: session-timing

session_times <- data$task_meta_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(subj_id %in% data_params$subj_id)  |> 
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id, session_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(session_start = min(start_time), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(subj_id, session_start)

# calculate days between first and second session for each subject
days_between <- session_times |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id) |>
  dplyr::filter(n() >= 2) |>  # only subjects with two sessions
  dplyr::summarise(
    first_session = min(session_start),
    second_session = nth(session_start, 2),
    days_between = as.numeric(difftime(second_session, first_session, units = "days")),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# calculate the average
average_days <- mean(days_between$days_between, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_days <- sd(days_between$days_between, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The average number of days between sessions one and two was `r sprintf("%.3f", round(average_days, 3))`, with a standard deviation of `r sprintf("%.0f", round(sd_days, 3))`.

Next, compute the average task duration for both sessions.

```{r}
#| label: task-duration

# calculate average task duration for first and second sessions separately
session_durations <- data$task_meta_data |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id, session_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(session_duration = sum(as.numeric(task_duration)), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(subj_id, session_id) |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id) |>
  dplyr::filter(n() >= 2) |>  # Only subjects with at least 2 sessions
  dplyr::mutate(session_order = row_number()) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

# calculate averages for each session
first_session_avg <- session_durations |>
  dplyr::filter(session_order == 1) |>
  dplyr::summarise(avg_duration = mean(session_duration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(avg_duration)

second_session_avg <- session_durations |>
  dplyr::filter(session_order == 2) |>
  dplyr::summarise(avg_duration = mean(session_duration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(avg_duration)


print(paste("Average duration of first session task:", round(first_session_avg / 60, 3), "minutes"))
print(paste("Average duration of second session task:", round(second_session_avg / 60, 3), "minutes"))
```

The average task completion duration was `r sprintf("%.3f", round(first_session_avg / 60, 3))` minutes for the 1st session, and `r sprintf("%.0f", round(second_session_avg / 60, 3))` minutes for the 2nd session.

The two sesions of participants were scheduled for the same time of day to address potential confounding time-of-day/chronobiology effects on effort-based decision-making.

```{r}
#| label: session-time-of-day

# Compare times of day between sessions within participants
time_comparison <- session_times |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id) |>
  dplyr::filter(n() >= 2) |>  # Only subjects with at least 2 sessions
  dplyr::arrange(session_start) |>
  dplyr::mutate(session_order = row_number()) |>
  dplyr::filter(session_order <= 2) |>  # Only first two sessions
  dplyr::select(subj_id, session_order, session_start) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = session_order, values_from = session_start, names_prefix = "session_") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    time_of_day_1 = as.numeric(format(session_1, "%H")) + as.numeric(format(session_1, "%M"))/60,
    time_of_day_2 = as.numeric(format(session_2, "%H")) + as.numeric(format(session_2, "%M"))/60,
    time_difference = abs(time_of_day_2 - time_of_day_1)
  ) |>
  # Handle times that cross midnight (e.g., 23:00 vs 01:00)
  dplyr::mutate(
    time_difference = ifelse(time_difference > 12, 24 - time_difference, time_difference)
  )

print("\n--- Time of Day Comparison ---")
avg_time_diff <- mean(time_comparison$time_difference, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_time_diff <- sd(time_comparison$time_difference, na.rm = TRUE)

print(paste("Average time difference between sessions:", round(avg_time_diff, 3), "hours"))
print(paste("Standard deviation of time differences:", round(sd_time_diff, 3), "hours"))
print(paste("Average time difference in minutes:", round(avg_time_diff * 60, 3), "minutes"))
```

```{r}
#| label: condition-descriptives
#| warning: false

# function for processing condition data 
process_conditions <- function(prefix, condition_name) {
  # Get condition columns (only logical)
  cond_data <- data_params |>
    dplyr::select(starts_with(paste0(prefix, "_conditions_"))) |>
    dplyr::select(where(is.logical))
  
  # calculate counts for specific conditions
  cond_counts <- cond_data |>
    dplyr::summarise(across(everything(), sum, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "condition", values_to = "n") |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      condition = str_remove(condition, paste0(prefix, "_conditions_")),
      condition = str_to_title(str_replace_all(condition, "_", " ")),
      percent = n/nrow(data_params)*100,
      display = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, percent)
    )
  
  # return both total and specific counts
  list(
    total = sum(data_params[[paste0(prefix, "_conditions")]], na.rm = TRUE),
    conditions = cond_counts
  )
}

# process neurological condition data
neuro_data <- process_conditions("neuro", "Neurological Conditions") 
# rename conditions 
neuro_data$conditions %<>%
  dplyr::mutate(condition = case_when(condition == "Ms" ~ "Multiple sclerosis",
                               condition == "Tbi" ~ "Traumatic brain injury",
                               condition == "Headache" ~ "Headache disorder",
                               condition == "Parkinsons" ~ "Parkinson's disease",
                               TRUE ~ condition))

# process mental/neurodev condition data
mh_data <- process_conditions("mh", "Mental Health Conditions")
mh_data$conditions %<>%
  dplyr::mutate(condition = case_when(
    condition == "Mdd" ~ "Major depressive disorder",
    condition == "Gad" ~ "Generalised anxiety disorder",
    condition == "Ocd" ~ "Obsessive compulsive disorder",
    condition == "Bipolar" ~ "Bipolar disorder",
    TRUE ~ condition,
  ))

# create conditions table
health_table <- bind_rows(
  # neurological conditions
  tibble(
    Condition = "Neurological Conditions",
    `n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", neuro_data$total, neuro_data$total/nrow(data_params)*100)
  ),
  # populate the table
  neuro_data$conditions |> dplyr::mutate(Condition = paste0("  ", condition)) |> dplyr::select(Condition, `n (%)` = display),
  
  # mental and neurodevelopmental conditions
  tibble(
    Condition = "Mental Health and Neurodevelopmental Conditions",
    `n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", mh_data$total, mh_data$total/nrow(data_params)*100)
  ),
  # populate the table
  mh_data$conditions |> dplyr::mutate(Condition = paste0("  ", condition)) |> dplyr::select(Condition, `n (%)` = display)
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 2**"),
    subtitle = "Reported Health Conditions"
  ) |>
  # formatting across rows 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = !str_starts(Condition, "  "))
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(1), color = "black"),
```

None of the included participants reported having any neurological condition, and 9 (9.2%) of participants reported lifetime diagnosis of a mental health or neurodevelopmental condition.

## Assumption checks

Examine the assumptions of statistical tests and apply transformation for meaningful interpretation of data.

```{r}
#| label: assumption1

# assumption 1: No outliers in the difference between the groups
data_params |>
  dplyr::mutate(wl_difference = wl_tiktok - wl_netflix) |>
  dplyr::select(wl_difference) |>
  rstatix::identify_outliers()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-box-wantlike
#| fig-cap: "Boxplot for wanting-liking difference between conditions"
#| fig-align: left
#| out-width: "95%"

data_params |>
  dplyr::mutate(wl_difference = wl_tiktok - wl_netflix) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = wl_difference)) +
  geom_boxplot()

```

@fig-box-wantlike illustrates the few outliers in the group difference.

```{r}
#| label: assumption2

# assumption 2: Normal distribution of the difference pairs (Shapiro-Wilk test)
data_params |>
  dplyr::mutate(wl_difference = wl_tiktok - wl_netflix) |>
  rstatix::shapiro_test(wl_difference)
```

The Shapiro-wilk test is non-significant, indicating that the distribution of the wanting-liking difference pairs (between TikTok and Netflix condition) approximates normal.

To further examine this, I visualise the QQ-plots for the wanting-liking difference for each condition separately.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq-comparison
#| fig-cap: "QQ-plots for TikTok and Netflix"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: "95%"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "TikTok QQ-plot"
#|   - "Netflix QQ-plot"

p1 <- ggpubr::ggqqplot(data_params, x = "wl_tiktok") + 
  ggtitle("TikTok") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p2 <- ggpubr::ggqqplot(data_params, x = "wl_netflix") + 
  ggtitle("Netflix") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p1 + p2
```

@fig-qq-comparison QQ-plots indicate that the distribution of wanting-liking differences for both conditions are more narrow than that of a normal distribution. These deviations do not look substantial enough to warrant transformation of the data.

# Behaviour Analyses

Perform a mixed-effects ANOVA to examine the effect of effort discounting.

```{r}
#| label: mixed-effects-anova

choice_data <- data$task_data |>
  dplyr::filter(subj_id %in% data_params$subj_id) |>
  dplyr::filter(offerReward != 999) |>
  # acceptance probability per subject, effort level, and reward level
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id, offerEffort, offerReward) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_choice = mean(choice))

anova(nlme::lme(mean_choice ~ offerEffort * offerReward, random= ~1|subj_id, data = choice_data))
```

The mixed-effects ANOVA confirms a main effect of effort and reward, as well as the interaction between the two on acceptance probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: task-accepted-sucess-rate

# rate of accepted challenges
data$task_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(phase == "game") |> 
  # accepted trials
  dplyr::filter(choice == 1) |> 
  group_by(subj_id) |> 
  reframe(prop_accept = n() / 128) |> 
  reframe(mean_prop_accept = mean(prop_accept)*100, 
          sd_prop_accept = sd(prop_accept)*100, 
          min_prop_accept = min(prop_accept), 
          max_prop_accept = max(prop_accept))

# successrate of accepted challenges
p_succ <- data$task_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(phase == "game") |> 
  # accepted trials
  dplyr::filter(choice == 1) |> 
  group_by(subj_id) |> 
  reframe(prop_success = sum((goalClicks - clicks) <= 0) / n()) |> 
  reframe(mean_prop_sucess = mean(prop_success)*100, 
          sd_prop_sucess = sd(prop_success)*100)
```

The modeling procedure utilises all trials without regard for the fact whether participants accept trials that they end up failing. A look at the data reveals that participants fail close to no offers that they accept: `r sprintf("%.3f", p_succ[1])`

We can also look at the acceptance rates for each of the two conditions.

```{r}
#| label: trial-behaviour

# Netflix condition
netflix_results <- data$task_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(phase == "game") |> 
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(session_id, "netflix")) |> 
  # accepted trials
  dplyr::filter(choice == 1) |> 
  group_by(subj_id) |> 
  reframe(prop_accept = n() / 64) |> 
  reframe(
    condition = "Netflix",
    mean_prop_accept = mean(prop_accept) * 100, 
    sd_prop_accept = sd(prop_accept) * 100, 
    min_prop_accept = min(prop_accept) * 100, 
    max_prop_accept = max(prop_accept) * 100
  )

# TikTok condition
tiktok_results <- data$task_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(phase == "game") |> 
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(session_id, "tiktok")) |> 
  # accepted trials
  dplyr::filter(choice == 1) |> 
  group_by(subj_id) |> 
  reframe(prop_accept = n() / 64) |> 
  reframe(
    condition = "TikTok",
    mean_prop_accept = mean(prop_accept) * 100, 
    sd_prop_accept = sd(prop_accept) * 100, 
    min_prop_accept = min(prop_accept) * 100, 
    max_prop_accept = max(prop_accept) * 100
  )

# combine results
combined_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(netflix_results, tiktok_results)

# print with formatting
combined_results |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(mean_prop_accept:max_prop_accept, ~ round(., 2))
  ) |> 
  dplyr::select(
    Condition = condition,
    `Mean (%)` = mean_prop_accept,
    `SD (%)` = sd_prop_accept,
    `Min (%)` = min_prop_accept,
    `Max (%)` = max_prop_accept
  )
```

Beyond the above description, let's test this formally.

```{r}
#| label: acceptance-bayestest

# calculate acceptance proportions per participant
acceptance_props <- data$task_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(phase == "game") |> 
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(session_id, "netflix|tiktok")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(choice == 1) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    condition = dplyr::case_when(
      stringr::str_detect(session_id, "netflix") ~ "netflix",
      stringr::str_detect(session_id, "tiktok") ~ "tiktok"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id, condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(prop_accept = n() / 64, .groups = "drop") |> 
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = condition,
    values_from = prop_accept,
    names_prefix = "prop_"
  )

# calculate means for reporting
netflix_mean <- mean(acceptance_props$prop_netflix, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
tiktok_mean <- mean(acceptance_props$prop_tiktok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100

# Bayesian paired t-test
bf_result <- ttestBF(
  x = acceptance_props$prop_netflix,
  y = acceptance_props$prop_tiktok,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = "medium"  # Cauchy prior width (medium = sqrt(2)/2 ≈ 0.707)
)

# Extract results
bf_value <- extractBF(bf_result)[1, "bf"]
bf_value

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(bf_result, iterations = 10000)

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF10*** **of `r round(bf_value, 3)`** indicates strong support for the null hypothesis that acceptance rates did not differ between the TikTok and Netflix conditions within subjects. The *95% Credible Interval* of the condition difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

```{r}

# accepted challenges plot

                             plot_type = "line_plot",
                             arrange_cols = 0, arrange_rows = 0) +
  labs(x = "Effort level", y = "Acceptance probability (SE)") +
  theme_custom()

acceptance_plot

# save rds
saveRDS(acceptance_plot, here::here("output", "rds", "gg_taskbehaviour_exp1.rds"))

# save ggplot
ggsave(
  acceptance_plot,
  filename = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1", "task_behaviour.png"),
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 800,
  background = "white"
)
```

# Main Analyses

## Hypothesis 1

*Hypothesis 1:* *Wanting* (acceptance bias parameter) is higher for TikTok than for Netflix.

Below, I perform a Bayesian paired samples t-test on the choice bias parameter (a), testing for differences between the TikTok and Netflix condition within subject.

```{r}
#| label: hypothesis1

# Bayesian paired samples t-test
tbf <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$a_tiktok,
  data_params$a_netflix,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf <- exp(tbf@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "delta"])
estimated_correlation_med <- median(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r round(bf, 3)`** indicates moderate support for the null hypothesis that *wanting* is the same for the TikTok and Netflix conditions within subjects. The *95% Credible Interval* of the condition difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`, with a median estimate of `r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation_med)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-params-want
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of wanting parameter (a)"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

# wanting (a) distribution 
medians_want <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(a_tiktok, a_netflix),
               names_to = "condition",
               values_to = "liking") |>
  dplyr::group_by(condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_val = median(liking, na.rm = TRUE))

p_w_dens <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c("a_tiktok", "a_netflix"),

  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = acceptance_bias, group = condition, fill = condition)) +
    ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = .7, outline.type = "lower", colour = NA) +
  ggdist::stat_interval(
    aes(y = -0.02, colour = condition),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.02),
    orientation = "horizontal",
    linewidth = 3,
    alpha = 0.3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = medians_want,
    aes(x = median_val, y = -0.02, fill = condition, colour = condition),
    size = 2,
    shape = 19,
    alpha = 1,
    stroke = 1,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.02, orientation = "y"),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(x = "Wanting (TikTok)", y = "Wanting (Netflix)") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", labels = c("a_tiktok" = "TikTok", "a_netflix" = "Netflix"), begin = 0.3, end = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", labels = c("a_tiktok" = "TikTok", "a_netflix" = "Netflix"), begin = 0.3, end = 0.7) +
  theme_custom() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3.5, 6.5), breaks = seq(-3,6,3)) +

# liking (strap-r) distribution
medians_like <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(strap_tiktok_avg, strap_netflix_avg),
               names_to = "condition",
               values_to = "liking") |>
  dplyr::group_by(condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_val = median(liking, na.rm = TRUE))

p_l_dens <- data_params |>

    cols = c("strap_tiktok_avg", "strap_netflix_avg"),

p_wl_dens <- ggpubr::ggarrange(

saveRDS(p_l_dens, file = here::here("output", "rds", "gg_liking_exp1.rds"))
saveRDS(p_w_dens, file = here::here("output", "rds", "gg_wanting_exp1.rds"))

ggsave(plot = p_wl_dens, filename = "density_wantingliking.png", device = "png", path = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1"), dpi = 800, bg = "white")
```

As shown in @fig-params-want, the distributions of the wanting parameter show large overlap between the TikTok and Netflix conditions. For self-reported liking, as demonstrated in panel B, Netflix was rated substantially higher on average.

The prior and posterior distributions for the Bayesian paired samples t-test on the wanting parameter are visualised below, and demonstrate the change in belief with regard to the effect of condition on wanting (a) after observing the data. The prior distribution is a Cauchy distribution with a scale of 1/3.

```{r}
#| label: fig-h1-prior
#| fig-cap: "Prior and posterior distributions for the effect of condition on wanting (a) for Hypothesis 1"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

# draw posterior samples
posterior_samples_h1 <- posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)

# extract delta standaridsed effect size
delta_samples_h1 <- posterior_samples_h1[, "delta"]

# Plot prior and posterior distributions for Hypothesis 1
delta_range <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)
prior_density <- dcauchy(delta_range, location = 0, scale = 1/3)

plot_data <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range,
  prior = prior_density
)

ggplot_h1 <- ggplot() +
  # posterior
  geom_density(data = data.frame(delta = delta_samples_h1),
               aes(x = delta_samples_h1, fill = "Posterior"), 
               alpha = 0.7,
               colour = NA) +
  # prior
  geom_line(data = plot_data,
            aes(x = delta, y = prior, color = "Prior"),
            linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.9, end = 0.8, name = NULL, direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Effect size (δ)", 
       y = "Density",
       title = "") + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1,1)) +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(0.125, .925),
        legend.background = element_blank(),
        legend.key = element_blank())

print(ggplot_h1)

ggsave(
  filename = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1", "analyses", "fig-h1-prior-posterior.png"),
  plot = ggplot_h1, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 800, bg = "white"
)
```

@fig-h1-prior presents the prior to posterior distributions for the effect of condition on wanting (a) for Hypothesis 1. The posterior distribution shows a shift towards zero, indicating that the data provide evidence in favor of the null hypothesis of no difference in wanting between conditions. The prior distribution is wider, reflecting more uncertainty about the effect size before observing the data, while the posterior is more concentrated around zero, reflecting increased certainty about the lack of an effect after observing the data.

### Hypothesis 1 explore

We explore individual-level variation below, specifically examining whether liking and wanting ratings show variation within individuals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distr
#| fig-cap: "Subject liking estimates"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

p_like <- data_params |> ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = strap_tiktok_avg, y = strap_netflix_avg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_abline() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "TikTok liking", 
    y = "Netflix liking"
  ) +
  theme_custom() + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1,7), breaks = 1:7)

p_want <- data_params |> ggplot(aes(x = a_tiktok, y = a_netflix)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_abline() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "TikTok wanting", 
    y = "Netflix wanting"
  ) +
  theme_custom() + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-4, 6.5), breaks = -4:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-4,6.6), breaks = -4:6)

combined_plot <- ggpubr::ggarrange(
  p_like, p_want,
  ncol = 2,
  labels = c("A", "B"),
  common.legend = TRUE,
  legend = "bottom"
)

print(combined_plot)
```

@fig-distr illustrates the liking and wanting values for TikTok and Netflix for individual participants. Deviations from the identity line indicate differences between the two conditions.

We proceed to statistically examine the above variation in liking between the two conditions. We perform a bayesian paired t-test on the liking ratings for the TikTok and Netflix conditions, testing for differences within subjects.

```{r}
#| label: bfttest-liking

# Bayesian paired samples t-test
tbf <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$strap_tiktok_avg,
  data_params$strap_netflix_avg,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf <- exp(tbf@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- median(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r round(bf, 3)`** indicates extreme support for the alternative hypothesis that *liking* is different for the TikTok and Netflix conditions. The median standardised effect size (δ) is **`r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation)`**. The *95% Credible Interval* of the group difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

#### Liking measurement stability or trajectories

Liking was assessed using a single-item self-report measure implemented three times throughout the waiting period. It is plausible that liking ratings may show variation across the three measurement occasions. To explore this, we visualise the trajectories of TikTok liking ratings across the three measurement occasions for each participant and condition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distr-subj
#| fig-cap: "Subject liking estimates"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

trajectory_data <- data_params |>
  dplyr::select(subj_id, strap_tiktok_1, strap_tiktok_2, strap_tiktok_3) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("strap_tiktok"), 
               names_to = "time_point", 
               values_to = "strap_score") |>
  dplyr::mutate(time_point = case_when(
    time_point == "strap_tiktok_1" ~ 1,
    time_point == "strap_tiktok_2" ~ 2,
    time_point == "strap_tiktok_3" ~ 3
  ))

# create the trajectory plot
trajectory_plot <- ggplot(trajectory_data, aes(x = time_point, y = strap_score, group = subj_id, color = subj_id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  stat_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "loess", se = TRUE, 
              color = "gray15", fill = "gray30", linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", begin = 0.1, end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2, 3), 
                     labels = c("Time 1", "Time 2", "Time 3")) +
  labs(x = "Measurement Occasion",
       y = "Liking") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme_custom() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray60"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

print(trajectory_plot)
```

@fig-distr-subj shows variation across mesurement occasions but no systematic trends or drifts that would suggest taking an average of the three liking measures would mask interesting variation in subsequent analyses.

#### Within-subject trajectories of wanting across conditions

Similar to liking, we examine individual variation in differences of wanting between the TikTok and Netflix condition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-a-within
#| fig-cap: "Wanting within subjects"
#| out-width: "95%"

data_with_slopes <- data_params |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(a_tiktok, a_netflix), names_to = "conditions1", values_to = "values") |>
  dplyr::mutate(conditions1_numeric = ifelse(conditions1 == "a_tiktok", 0, 1)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(subj_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    slope = ifelse(n() > 1, 
                   (values[conditions1_numeric == 1] - values[conditions1_numeric == 0]) / 
                   (1 - 0), 
                   0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  right_join(
    data_params |> 
      pivot_longer(cols = c(a_tiktok, a_netflix), names_to = "conditions1", values_to = "values"),
    by = "subj_id"
  ) 

# Create the plot with slope-based coloring (positive vs negative)
data_with_slopes |>
  dplyr::mutate(slope_direction = ifelse(slope > 0, "Negative", "Positive")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = values, x = conditions1, colour = slope_direction)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line(aes(group = subj_id)) + 
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = "Slope") +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Condition", labels = c("Netflix", "TikTok")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Wanting") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme_custom() 
```

@fig-a-within illustrates the estimated wanting parameter within individuals to examine whether we can observe within-subject variation in wanting with respect to the two platforms, as opposed to measuring more trait-like motivational tendencies across contexts.

## Hypothesis 2

*Hypothesis 2:* The dissociation of *wanting* (acceptance bias parameter) and *liking* (momentary self-report) is higher for TikTok than for Netflix.

I perform a Bayesian paired samples t-test on the wanting-liking difference, testing for differences between the TikTok and Netflix condition within subjects.

```{r}
#|label: hypothesis2

# Bayesian paired t-test
tbf_diff <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$wl_tiktok,
  data_params$wl_netflix,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf <- exp(tbf_diff@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf_diff, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "delta"])
estimated_correlation <- median(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r sprintf("%.3f", bf)`** indicates very strong support in favour of the alternative hypothesis, that the wanting-liking difference is larger for TikTok than Netflix. The median standardised effect size (δ) is **`r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation)`**. The *95% Credible Interval* of the group difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-params-wantlike
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of wanting-liking difference"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

# wanting-liking distribution
medians <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(wl_tiktok_z, wl_netflix_z),
               names_to = "condition",
               values_to = "want_like_difference") |>
  dplyr::group_by(condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_val = median(want_like_difference, na.rm = TRUE))

p_wl_diff_dens <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c("wl_tiktok_z", "wl_netflix_z"),
    names_to = "condition",
    values_to = "want_like_difference"
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = want_like_difference, group = condition, fill = condition)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = .7, outline.type = "lower", colour = NA) +
  ggdist::stat_interval(
    aes(y = -0.025, colour = condition),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.04),
    orientation = "horizontal",
    linewidth = 3,
    alpha = 0.4,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = medians,
    aes(x = median_val, y = -0.025, fill = condition, colour = condition),
    size = 2,
    shape = 19,
    alpha = 1,
    stroke = 1,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.04, orientation = "y"),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", labels = c("wl_tiktok_z" = "TikTok", "wl_netflix_z" = "Netflix"), begin = 0.3, end = 0.7 ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", labels = c("wl_tiktok_z" = "TikTok", "wl_netflix_z" = "Netflix"), begin = 0.3, end = 0.7) +
  theme_custom() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(NA, NA), breaks = seq(-4,4,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.05, 0.45), breaks = seq(0, 0.4, 0.1)) +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(0.125, 0.925),
        legend.background = element_blank(),
        legend.key = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Wanting-liking dissocation (z)", y = "Density", fill = "Condition")

saveRDS(p_wl_diff_dens, file = here::here("output", "rds", "gg_wantlike_exp1.rds"))

p_param_dens <- ggpubr::ggarrange(
  p_w_dens, p_l_dens, p_wl_diff_dens,
  ncol = 3, nrow = 1,
  labels = c("A", "B", "C"),
  common.legend = TRUE,
  legend = "bottom"
)

ggsave(plot = p_param_dens, filename = "density_wanting_liking.png", device = "png", path = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1"), dpi = 800, width = 10, height = 5, bg = "white")

print(p_wl_diff_dens)
```

@fig-params-wantlike illustrates the distribution of the *wanting-liking dissociation* for the TikTok and Netflix conditions. For interpretation purposes, we show the z-transformed difference scores. A larger value of the *wanting-liking dissociation* indicates higher wanting relative to liking, and a lower score indicates less dissociation or higher liking relative to wanting.

We present the prior and posterior distributions for the Bayesian paired samples t-test on the wanting-liking difference, demonstrating the change in belief with regard to the effect of condition on the wanting-liking dissociation after observing the data. The prior distribution is a Cauchy distribution with a scale of 1/3.

```{r}
#| label: fig-h2-prior

# draw posterior samples
posterior_samples_h2 <- posterior(tbf_diff, iterations = 10000)

# extract delta standaridsed effect size
delta_samples_h2 <- posterior_samples_h2[, "delta"]

# Plot prior and posterior distributions for Hypothesis 1
delta_range <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)
prior_density <- dcauchy(delta_range, location = 0, scale = 1/3)

plot_data <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range,
  prior = prior_density
)

ggplot_h2 <- ggplot() +
  # Posterior
  geom_density(data = data.frame(delta = delta_samples_h2),
               aes(x = delta_samples_h2, fill = "Posterior"), 
               alpha = 0.7,
               colour = NA) +
  # Prior
  geom_line(data = plot_data,
            aes(x = delta, y = prior, color = "Prior"),
            linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.9, end = 0.8, name = NULL, direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Effect size (δ)", 
       y = "Density",
       title = "") + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,4)) +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(0.125, .925),
        legend.background = element_blank(),
        legend.key = element_blank())

print(ggplot_h2)

ggsave(
  filename = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1", "analyses", "fig-h2-prior-posterior.png"),
  plot = ggplot_h2, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 800, bg = "white"
)
```

#### Hypothesis 2 explore

Below, we examine whether the wanting-liking dissociation is driven by differences in *wanting* or *liking* between the TikTok and Netflix conditions. To this end, I construct a multivariate model that includes condition as a predictor and random intercepts for subjects (to reflect the paired nature of the data).

```{r}
#| label: multivariate-model
#| cache: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: false

# format data in long
data_params_long <- data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(wl_netflix, wl_tiktok, a_netflix, a_tiktok, strap_netflix_avg, strap_tiktok_avg),
    names_to = c(".value", "condition"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

data_params_long <- data_params_long |>
  mutate(
    a_scaled = scale(a),
    strap_scaled = scale(strap)
  )

mv_model <- brms::brm(
  mvbind(a_scaled, strap_scaled) ~ condition + (1|subj_id),
  data = data_params_long,
  family = gaussian(),
  cores = 4,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 500,
  control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.95)
)

# save model parameters for referencing
model_params <- brms::fixef(mv_model)  # fixed effects
model_ranef <- brms::VarCorr(mv_model) # random effects
```

Let's examine the returned estimates, split by random and fixed effects.

**Random Effects:**

*sd(a_Intercept)* = `r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[1]])`, with the *95% CI* \[`r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[5]])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[7]])`\]. This indicates that there is substantial between-subject variability in *wanting*.

*sd(strap_Intercept)* = `r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[2]])`, with the *95% CI* \[`r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[6]])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", model_ranef$subj_id$sd[[8]])`\]. This indicates that between-subject variability in *liking* is smaller but present.

**Fixed Effects:**

*a_Intercept* = `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[1]])`, with the *95% CI* \[`r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[9]])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[13]])`\]. This quantifies the average estimated *wanting* in the reference condition (Netflix).

*a_conditiontiktok* = `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[3]])`, with the *95% CI* \[`r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[11]])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[15]])`\]. The difference in "wanting" for TikTok compared to Netflix. The 95% credible interval includes zero, suggesting no clear evidence of a difference in wanting between platforms.

*stap_conditiontiktok* = `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[4]])`, with the *95% CI* \[`r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[12]])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", model_params[[16]])`\]. The difference in "liking" for TikTok compared to Netflix. The 95% credible interval does not include zero, suggesting a clear difference in liking between platforms.

The estimates are visualised below, and indicate that the *wanting-liking dissociation* is driven by differences in *liking* between the two conditions, and not the *wanting* parameter.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multivariate-effects
#| fig-cap: "Effect sumamry of multivariate model"
#| out-width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# extract coefficients
coef_data <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Wanting (TikTok vs. Netflix)", "Liking (TikTok vs. Netflix)"),
  Estimate = fixef(mv_model)[3:4, "Estimate"],
  lower = fixef(mv_model)[3:4, "Q2.5"],
  upper = fixef(mv_model)[3:4, "Q97.5"]
)

# Create a forest plot
ggplot2::ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = Estimate, y = Parameter)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Effect size",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11)
  )
```

@fig-multivariate-effects shows the effect summary of the multivariate model, including the outcomes *wanting* and *liking* and the predictor condition.

## Hypothesis 3

*Hypothesis 3a:* The dissociation between *wanting* (acceptance bias parameter) and *liking* (momentary self-report) of TikTok is related to addiction severity (Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, TikTok).

I perform a Bayesian correlation using the behavioural proxy of addiction (wanting-liking dissociation) and the self-reported addiction scale values for each participant.

```{r}
#| label: hypothesis3tiktok
#| cache: false

# TikTok: Bayesian correlation
tbf_corr_tiktok <- BayesFactor::correlationBF(
  data_params$wl_tiktok,
  data_params$bsmas_tiktok_total,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf_tiktok <- exp(tbf_corr_tiktok@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf_corr_tiktok, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for rho
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "rho"])
estimated_correlation_med <- median(posterior_samples[, "rho"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "rho"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r sprintf("%.3f", bf_tiktok)`** indicates support for the null hypothesis that the TikTok wanting-liking dissociation does not relate to the corresponding self-reported addiction score.

The correlation estimate (median) is **`r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation_med)`**. Given that larger dissociation between wanting and liking are more negative values, one would expect a negative correlation between wanting-liking dissociations and the self-reported addiction measure. The *95% Credible Interval* of this correlation ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

#### Hypothesis 3b: Netflix

*Hypothesis 3b:* The dissociation between *wanting* (acceptance bias parameter) and *liking* (momentary self-report) of Netflix is related to addiction severity (Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, Netflix).

```{r}
#| label: hypothesis3netflix
#| cache: false

# Netflix: Bayesian correlation
tbf_corr_netflix <- BayesFactor::correlationBF(
  data_params$wl_netflix,
  data_params$bsmas_netflix_total,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf_netflix <- exp(tbf_corr_netflix@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf_corr_netflix, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for rho
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "rho"])
estimated_correlation_med <- median(posterior_samples[, "rho"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "rho"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r sprintf("%.3f", bf_netflix)`** indicates inconclusive evidence with respect to the null hypothesis that the Netflix wanting-liking dissociation does not relate to the corresponding BSMAS score.

The correlation estimate of the Bayesian correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation_med)`. Given that larger dissociations between wanting and liking are more negative values, one would expect a negative correlation between wanting-liking dissociations and the self-reported addiction measure. The *95% Credible Interval* of this correlation ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bsmas-wl
#| fig-cap: "Association between Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale and Want-like dissociation"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

mainplot <- data_params |>
  # create a longer format dataset that includes both Netflix and TikTok data
  tidyr::pivot_longer(

  # only keep matching rows (Netflix with Netflix, TikTok with TikTok)

    (platform_wl == "wl_netflix_z" & platform_bsmas == "bsmas_netflix_total") |
    (platform_wl == "wl_tiktok_z" & platform_bsmas == "bsmas_tiktok_total")
  ) |>
  # create a clean platform variable
  dplyr::mutate(
    platform = dplyr::case_when(
      platform_wl == "wl_netflix_z" ~ "Netflix",
      platform_wl == "wl_tiktok_z" ~ "TikTok"
    )

  # create plot
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = bsmas_score, x = want_like, color = platform)) +
 # scatterplot with jitter for visibility

    width = 0.45,

    height = 0.15,

    shape = 19,

  ) +
    # regression line - one per platform

              method = "lm", se = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE,
              linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.25, linetype = "solid") +
  # Add regression equation - one per platform

    aes(group = platform, color = platform,

    name = NULL,
    alpha = 0.4,
    guide = "none", labels = c("wl_tiktok_z" = "TikTok", "wl_netflix_z" = "Netflix")) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL, 
                         labels = c("wl_tiktok_z" = "TikTok", "wl_netflix_z" = "Netflix")) +
  theme_custom() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 30, 5), limits = c(5,30)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 4, 1)) +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(0.125, 0.925),
        legend.background = element_blank(),
        legend.key = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Wanting-Liking dissociation (z)", y = "Self-reported addiction", fill = "Condition")

saveRDS(mainplot, file = here::here("output", "rds", "gg_wlbsmas_exp1.rds"))

# remove legens from individual plots for merging with ggmarginal object
p_w_dens_no_legend <- p_w_dens +

p_l_dens_no_legend <- p_l_dens +

p_wl_diff_dens_no_legend <- p_wl_diff_dens +

# merge plots with ggarrange

print(p_param_dens)
```

# Exploratory Analyses

## Control variables

The above findings indicate that the *wanting-liking dissociation* is more pronounced for TikTok than Netflix. In the below, I examine whether this remains true when accounting for *gender* and *age* of participants.

```{r}
#| label: h2-control-demo
#| cache: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| error: false
#| output: false

# fit Bayesian mixed model with age and sex as covariates
model_demographic <- brms::brm(
  wl ~ condition + age + gender + (1|subj_id),
  data = data_params_long,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(0, 5), class = "b"),
    prior(cauchy(0, 2), class = "sd")
  ),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 10000,
  warmup = 500,
  cores = 4,
  control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.95)
)

# examine results
print(summary(model_demographic), digits = 3)

# extract platform effects after controlling for demographics
posterior_samples <- posterior_samples(model_demographic)
platform_effect <- posterior_samples$b_conditiontiktok  
mean_effect <- mean(platform_effect, na.rm = TRUE)
ci_effect <- quantile(platform_effect, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The average platform effect is `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_effect)`, 95% CI \[ `r sprintf("%.3f", ci_effect[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", ci_effect[2])`\], when controlling for age and gender. The model indicates no robust effects for age or gender. I visualise this below:

```{r}
#| label: fig-demographic-effects
#| fig-cap: "Effects of condition, age, and gender on wanting-liking dissociation"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "95%"

# extract coefficients
coef_data <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("TikTok (vs Netflix)", "Age (per year)", "Male (vs Female)", "Non-binary (vs Female)"),
  Estimate = fixef(model_demographic)[2:5, "Estimate"],
  lower = fixef(model_demographic)[2:5, "Q2.5"],
  upper = fixef(model_demographic)[2:5, "Q97.5"]
)

# Create a forest plot
ggplot2::ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = Estimate, y = Parameter)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Effect size",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11)
  )
```

@fig-demographic-effects shows the effect size of the predictors *condition*, *gender*, and *age*. We do not find differences based on gender or age, whereas condition shows a positive effect, with the dissociation being larger for TikTok than Netflix.

```{r}

#|fig-cap: "Distribution of wanting-liking dissociation across genders"

data_params |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = wl_tiktok_z, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .75) +

```

@fig-dem-corr illustrates the distribution of wanting-liking difference scores across genders.

### Addiction self-report

The above findings indicate that the wanting-liking dissociation is larger for TikTok than for Netflix. Let's examine the difference between participants ratings on the Bergen TikTok/Netflix Addiction Scale.

```{r}
#| label: self-report-comparison

# Bayesian paired t-test
tbf_bsmas <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$bsmas_tiktok_total,
  data_params$bsmas_netflix_total,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf <- exp(tbf_bsmas@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf_bsmas, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r sprintf("%.3f", bf)`** indicates weak support for the null hypothesis that Bergen self-report addiction scores are the same across the TikTok and Netflix adaptation of the scale. The *95% Credible Interval* of the group difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`. The respective distributions are displayed below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-difference-bsmas
#| fig-cap: "Bergen self-report addiction scores for TikTok and Netflix"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "95%"

# wanting-liking distribution
data_params |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c("bsmas_tiktok_total", "bsmas_netflix_total"),
    names_to = "condition",
    values_to = "bsmas_total"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(condition = as.factor(condition)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = bsmas_total, fill = condition)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(
    alpha = .7,
    show.legend = TRUE, outline.type = "lower", colour = NA
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL, labels = c("bsmas_tiktok_total" = "TikTok", "bsmas_netflix_total" = "Netflix")) +
  scale_pattern_angle_manual(
    values = c("bsmas_tiktok_total" = 45, "bsmas_netflix_total" = 90),
    guide = "none" # remove pattern legend
  ) +
  labs(x = "Self-reported social media addiction", y = "Density", fill = "Condition")
```

@fig-difference-bsmas shows the distribution of self-reported addiction scores for TikTok and Netflix.

### Computational parameters

Examine the correlations between other computational parameters (effort and reward sensitivity) and self-reported addiction measures.

```{r}
#| label: fig-params-bsmas

p_eff <- data_params |>

# remove legend from individual plots
```

@fig-params-bsmas illustrates the correlations between the different effort-based decision-making parameter estimates and individuals' scores on the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (TikTok, Netflix).

#### Condition differences in computational parameters

##### Reward sensitivity

```{r}
tbf <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$kR_tiktok,
  data_params$kR_netflix,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

bf <- exp(tbf@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "delta"])
estimated_correlation_med <- median(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

tbf_chains <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)
base::summary(tbf_chains)
plot(tbf_chains[, "delta"])
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r round(bf, 3)`** indicates moderate support for the null hypothesis that *reward sensitivity* does not differ between the TikTok and Netflix conditions within subjects. The *95% Credible Interval* of the condition difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

##### Effort sensitivity

```{r}
tbf <- BayesFactor::ttestBF(
  data_params$kE_tiktok,
  data_params$kE_netflix,
  paired = TRUE,
  rscale = 1/3
)

bf <- exp(tbf@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for delta
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "delta"])
estimated_correlation_med <- median(posterior_samples[, "delta"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "delta"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

tbf_chains <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf, iterations = 10000)
base::summary(tbf_chains)
plot(tbf_chains[, "delta"])
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r round(bf, 3)`** indicates weak support for the null hypothesis that *effort sensitivity* does not differ between the TikTok and Netflix conditions within subjects. The *95% Credible Interval* of the condition difference ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

```{r}

p_eff <- data_params |>
  # create a longer format dataset that includes both Netflix and TikTok data
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(kE_netflix,kE_tiktok),
    names_to = "platform_ke",
    values_to = "effort_sensitivity"
  ) |>
  # create plot
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = effort_sensitivity, fill = platform_ke)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .7, outline.type = "lower", colour = NA) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL,
    labels = c("kE_tiktok" = "TikTok", "kE_netflix" = "Netflix")
  ) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1,.2), limits = c(0,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,2,.5)) +
  theme(legend.position="right", legend.direction = "vertical") + 
  labs(x = "Effort sensitivity", y = "Density", fill = "Condition") 

p_rew <- data_params |>
  # create a longer format dataset that includes both Netflix and TikTok data
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(kR_netflix,kR_tiktok),
    names_to = "platform_kr",
    values_to = "reward_sensitivity"
  ) |>
  # create plot
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = reward_sensitivity, fill = platform_kr)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .7, outline.type = "lower", colour = NA) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7, name = NULL,
    labels = c("kR_tiktok" = "TikTok", "kR_netflix" = "Netflix")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,6,1), limits = c(0, 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1,.2), limits = c(0,0.6)) +
  labs(x = "Reward sensitivity", y = "Density", fill = "Condition")

# create combined plot
combined_plot <- ggpubr::ggarrange(
  p_rew, p_eff,
  ncol = 2,
  labels = c("A", "B"),
  common.legend = TRUE,
  legend = "right"
)

saveRDS(combined_plot, file = here::here("output", "rds", "kekr_parameter_distributions_exp1.rds"))

# save the main plot without legend

  filename = "kekr_parameter_distributions.png", 
  plot = combined_plot, 
  path = here::here("output", "figures", "experiment1"),
  dpi = 800, width = 10, height = 5, bg = "white"
)
```

Now, we perform the Bayesian correlation analyses with a default stretched beta prior (rscale = 1/3) to examine the evidence for associations between reward and effort sensitivity parameters and self-reported addiction scores.

### Reward sensitivity \~ Social media addiction

```{r}
#| label: bf-reward-bsmas
#| cache: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

tbf_corr_rew_tiktok <- BayesFactor::correlationBF(
  data_params$kR_tiktok,
  data_params$bsmas_tiktok_total,
  rscale = 1/3
)

# extract the Bayes factor value
bf_tiktok <- exp(tbf_corr_rew_tiktok@bayesFactor$bf)

# extract the posterior samples
posterior_samples <- BayesFactor::posterior(tbf_corr_rew_tiktok, iterations = 10000)

# calculate the mean of the posterior distribution for rho
estimated_correlation <- mean(posterior_samples[, "rho"])

# get 95% credible interval
credible_interval <- quantile(posterior_samples[, "rho"], probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The ***BF01*** **of `r sprintf("%.3f", bf_tiktok)`** indicates inconclusive evidence. The correlation estimate of the Bayesian correlation (median) is `r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation_med)`. The *95% Credible Interval* of this correlation ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

The correlation estimate of the Bayesian correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", estimated_correlation_med)`. The *95% Credible Interval* of this correlation ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", credible_interval[2])`.

These exploratory analyses are based on the variables introduced in earlier sections, and the additional variables *tiktok_screentime_avg* (objective time spent on TikTok via application settings), *tiktok_checking_frequency* (self-reported checking frequency on a Likert scale), and *tiktok_videos_watched* (objective read-out of number of videos watched during experiment waiting period).

```{r}
#| label: behaviour-correlate

# get the correlation coefficients and the p-values
corres1 <- cordat |> cor() 
cor_ps = as.data.frame(ggcorrplot::cor_pmat(cordat))
  
# function to get asteriks
labs.function = function(x){
  case_when(x >= 0.05 ~ "",
            x < 0.05 & x >= 0.01 ~ "*",
            x < 0.01 & x >= 0.001 ~ "**",
            x < 0.001 ~ "***")
} 

# extract asteriks based on p-values
p_labs = cor_ps  |>                      
  mutate_all(labs.function)

# reshape to match ggcorrplot formatting
p_labs$Var1 <- as.factor(rownames(p_labs))
p_labs <- reshape2::melt(p_labs, id.vars = "Var1", variable.name = "Var2", value.name = "lab")
  
cor_plot <-  ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot(corres1, hc.order = TRUE, type = "lower",
                      lab = TRUE)

# subsetting asteriks matrix
p_labs$in_df <- ifelse(is.na(match(paste0(p_labs$Var1, p_labs$Var2), 
                                  paste0(cor_plot[["data"]]$Var1, cor_plot[["data"]]$Var2))), "No", "Yes")

p_labs <- dplyr::select(dplyr::filter(p_labs, in_df == "Yes"), -in_df)

# add asteriks to ggcorrplot
cor_plot_labs = cor_plot +

                       breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.25),
                       name = "") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, 
                                   hjust = 1, 
                                   size = 12, 
                                   color = "black"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12, 
                                   color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_blank())

print(cor_plot_labs)
```

### RISQ Approach

We also included the Risq scale. Reminder, the Risq approach score specifically was assessed with the following item: "I do this behavior to feel excitement, to get a thrill, or to feel pleasure" rated on a five-point Likert scale. Let's examine the correlation between our wanting-liking dissociation and the risq scores.

```{r}
#| label: risq-correlation-with-want-like-tiktok
#| cache: false

# Netflix: Bayesian correlation
tbf_corr_risq_tiktok <- BayesFactor::correlationBF(
  data_params$wl_tiktok,
```

## Impulsivity (BIS-11)

The following sections present Bayesian correlation analyses which examine the relationship between the *wanting-liking* dissociation and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale and Subscales. The BIS-11 includes three subscales: non-planning, motor, and attention.

```{r}
#| label: data-preparation

# function: run Bayesian correlation analysis
run_bayesian_correlation <- function(x, y_vars, data, iterations = 10000) {
  # initiate empty store
  results <- list()
  
  # Loop through each y variable
  for (var in y_vars) {
    # compute correlation
    corr_bf <- BayesFactor::correlationBF(
      x = data[[x]],
      y = data[[var]],
      rscale = 1/3
    )
    
    # extract Bayesfactor
    bf_value <- exp(corr_bf@bayesFactor$bf)
    
    # extract posterior samples into matrix
    post_samples <- as.data.frame(BayesFactor::posterior(corr_bf, iterations = iterations))
    
    # calculate mean correlation
    corr_mean <- mean(post_samples$rho)
    
    # get credible intervals
    ci_lower <- stats::quantile(post_samples$rho, 0.025)
    ci_upper <- stats::quantile(post_samples$rho, 0.975)
    
    # calculate the probability of the correlation being larger than one
    prob_positive <- mean(post_samples$rho > 0)
    
    # store results
    results[[var]] <- list(
      bayes_factor = bf_value,
      correlation = corr_mean,
      ci_lower = ci_lower,
      ci_upper = ci_upper,
      prob_positive = prob_positive,
      samples = post_samples
    )
  }
  
  return(results)
}

# function: create summary tables
create_summary_table <- function(results) {
  var_names <- names(results)
  
  readable_names <- c(
    "bis_11_total" = "Total Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_nonplanning" = "Non-planning Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_motor" = "Motor Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_attention" = "Attentional Impulsivity"
  )
  
  summary_df <- data.frame(
    Variable = readable_names[var_names],
    Correlation = sapply(results, function(x) round(x$correlation, 3)),
    CI_Lower    = sapply(results, function(x) round(x$ci_lower, 3)),
    CI_Upper    = sapply(results, function(x) round(x$ci_upper, 3)),
    Bayes_Factor = sapply(results, function(x) round(x$bayes_factor, 3)),
    Prob_Positive = sapply(results, function(x) paste0(round(x$prob_positive * 100, 1), "%"))
  )
  
  return(summary_df)
}

# function: plot posteriors
plot_posteriors <- function(results, title = "") {
  # prepare data for plotting
  posterior_data <- data.frame()
  
  readable_names <- c(
    "bis_11_total" = "Total Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_nonplanning" = "Non-planning Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_motor" = "Motor Impulsivity",
    "bis_11_attention" = "Attentional Impulsivity"
  )
  
  for (var_name in names(results)) {
    # convert matrix of posteriors to dataframe
    samples_df <- as.data.frame(results[[var_name]]$samples)
    
    # extract correlation coefficients
    temp_data <- data.frame(
      rho = samples_df$rho,
      variable = readable_names[var_name]
    )
    posterior_data <- rbind(posterior_data, temp_data)
  }
  
  # create plot
  ggplot2::ggplot(posterior_data, ggplot2::aes(x = rho, fill = variable)) +
    ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Correlation coefficient (ρ)",
      y = "Density",
      fill = "Measure"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "C") +
    ggplot2::theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
      legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "plain")
    )
}

# function: interpret Bayesfactors
interpret_bf <- function(bf) {
  if (bf < 1/3) {
    return("Evidence favors null hypothesis")
  } else if (bf < 3) {
    return("Anecdotal evidence")
  } else if (bf < 10) {
    return("Moderate evidence for alternative")
  } else if (bf < 30) {
    return("Strong evidence for alternative")
  } else if (bf < 100) {
    return("Very strong evidence for alternative")
  } else {
    return("Extreme evidence for alternative")
  }
}
```

```{r}
  "bis_11_total",

  "bis_11_attention"
)

# TikTok analysis

  x = "wl_tiktok",

# Netflix analysis
netflix_results <- run_bayesian_correlation(
  x = "wl_netflix",
  y_vars = y_variables,
  data = data_params,
  iterations = 10000
)

# add interpretation column
tiktok_summary <- create_summary_table(tiktok_results)
tiktok_summary$Interpretation <- sapply(tiktok_summary$Bayes_Factor, interpret_bf)

netflix_summary <- create_summary_table(netflix_results)
netflix_summary$Interpretation <- sapply(netflix_summary$Bayes_Factor, interpret_bf)
```

```{r}
# Netflix strongest correlation
```

@tbl-wl shows the results of the Bayesian correlation analyses for self-reported addiction for TikTok and Netflix and the impulsivity measures.

**TikTok:** The Bayesian correlation analyses reveal that the *wanting-liking* dissociation is not correlated with the BIS-11 total score or any of the subscales. The strongest correlation is with `r tik_var` (ρ = `r tik_rho`, 95% CI \[`r tik_lower`, `r tik_upper`\]), with a Bayes Factor of `r tik_bf`, indicating `r tik_interp`.

**Netflix:** The Netflix correlation analysis shows that the *wanting-liking* dissociation is not correlated with the BIS-11 total score or any of the subscales. The strongest correlation is with `r net_var` (ρ = `r net_rho`, 95% CI \[`r net_lower`, `r net_upper`\]), with a Bayes Factor of `r net_bf`, indicating `r net_interp`.

#### Compare correlation coefficients across conditions

To directly compare how TikTok and Netflix usage relate to impulsivity, we created a combined visualization:

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of correlation strengths between platform usage and impulsivity measures"
#| out-width: "95%"

# prepare comparison of correlations
comparison_data <- data.frame(
  Measure = rep(tiktok_summary$Variable, 2),
  Platform = c(rep("TikTok", nrow(tiktok_summary)), rep("Netflix", nrow(netflix_summary))),
  Correlation = c(tiktok_summary$Correlation, netflix_summary$Correlation),
  CI_Lower = c(tiktok_summary$CI_Lower, netflix_summary$CI_Lower),
  CI_Upper = c(tiktok_summary$CI_Upper, netflix_summary$CI_Upper)
)

# order factors for plotting
comparison_data$Measure <- factor(comparison_data$Measure, 
                                 levels = c("Total Impulsivity", 
                                           "Attentional Impulsivity", 
                                           "Motor Impulsivity", 
                                           "Non-planning Impulsivity"))

# create comparison plot
ggplot2::ggplot(comparison_data, 
                ggplot2::aes(x = Measure, y = Correlation, fill = Platform)) +
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity", 
                   position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
                   width = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper), 
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
    width = 0.25
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("TikTok" = "black", "Netflix" = "red"), name = "Wanting-liking dissociation") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "", y = "Correlation (ρ)") +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "plain"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    text = element_text(size = 11)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::coord_flip()
```

@fig-comparison illustrates the differences in correlation strength between the two platforms across all impulsivity measures. Across Netflix and TikTok, the *wanting-liking* dissociation does not show substantial differences and/or correlations with the impulsivity measures. Let's visualise the data.

### Computational Parameters and Self-reported Addiction

Below, we examine correlations between other computational parameters (effort sensitivity, reward sensitivity) and self-reported levels of social media addiction (TikTok, BSMAS),

### Self-reported Addiction and Impulsivity

In the following, I examine the correlation between the self-reported TikTok and Netflix addiction scores (Bergen Scale) and the impulsivity measures.

```{r}
#| label: bsmas-impulsivity-analysis

# function: format data in long
prepare_data <- function(data_params) {
  data_params |>

    # format bsmas scores long
    tidyr::pivot_longer(
      cols = c(bsmas_netflix_total, bsmas_tiktok_total),
      names_to = "platform_bsmas",
      values_to = "bsmas_score"
    ) |>
    # only keep matching rows 
    dplyr::filter(
      (platform_bsmas == "bsmas_netflix_total") |
      (platform_bsmas == "bsmas_tiktok_total")
    ) |>
    # create a clean platform variable
    dplyr::mutate(
      platform = dplyr::case_when(
        platform_bsmas == "bsmas_netflix_total" ~ "Netflix",
        platform_bsmas == "bsmas_tiktok_total" ~ "TikTok"
      )
    )
}

# function: generate correlation plot
create_plot <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  data |>
    # create plot
    ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = bsmas_score, y = .data[[y_var]], color = platform)) +
    geom_jitter() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", begin = 0.3, end = 0.7) +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(
      x = "Self-reported addiction", 
      y = y_label,
      color = "Wanting-liking dissociation"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    # legend formatting
    guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "plain"),
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 30), breaks = seq(5, 30, 5))
}

# transform data
transformed_data <- prepare_data(data_params)

# TikTok analysis
tiktok_results <- run_bayesian_correlation(
  x = "bsmas_tiktok_total",
  y_vars = y_variables,
  data = data_params,
  iterations = 10000
)

# Netflix analysis
netflix_results <- run_bayesian_correlation(
  x = "bsmas_netflix_total",
  y_vars = y_variables,
  data = data_params,
  iterations = 10000
)

# add interpretation column
tiktok_summary <- create_summary_table(tiktok_results)
tiktok_summary$Interpretation <- sapply(tiktok_summary$Bayes_Factor, interpret_bf)

netflix_summary <- create_summary_table(netflix_results)
netflix_summary$Interpretation <- sapply(netflix_summary$Bayes_Factor, interpret_bf)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-merged-addiction
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian correlations between self-reported social media addiction and impulsivity measures"

  "Impulsivity Measure" = rep(tiktok_summary[,1], 2),
  "Correlation (ρ)" = c(tiktok_summary[,2], netflix_summary[,2]),
  "95% CI Lower" = c(tiktok_summary[,3], netflix_summary[,3]),
  "95% CI Upper" = c(tiktok_summary[,4], netflix_summary[,4]),
  "Bayes Factor (BF₁₀)" = c(tiktok_summary[,5], netflix_summary[,5]),
  "Prob(ρ > 0)" = c(tiktok_summary[,6], netflix_summary[,6]),
  "Interpretation" = c(tiktok_summary[,7], netflix_summary[,7])
)

# display merged table
kable(merged_summary, 
      col.names = c("Impulsivity Measure", "Correlation (ρ)", "95% CI Lower", 
                    "95% CI Upper", "Bayes Factor (BF₁₀)", 
                    "Prob(ρ > 0)", "Interpretation"),
      align = c("l", "l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "l")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), 
                full_width = TRUE, position = "center") |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#f5f5f5") |>
  # add background colours
  pack_rows("TikTok", 1, nrow(tiktok_summary), background = "#f8f9fa") |>
  pack_rows("Netflix", nrow(tiktok_summary) + 1, nrow(merged_summary), background = "#e9ecef")
```

@tbl-merged-addiction shows the results of the Bayesian correlation analyses for self-reported addiction for TikTok and Netflix and the impulsivity measures.

**TikTok:** The correlation analyses reveal that the self-reported addiction scores for TikTok are correlated with a subset of the impulsivity measures. The strongest correlation is with `r tiktok_summary$Variable[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]` (ρ = `r tiktok_summary$Correlation[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]`, 95% CI \[`r tiktok_summary$CI_Lower[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]`, `r tiktok_summary$CI_Upper[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]`\]), with a Bayes Factor of `r tiktok_summary$Bayes_Factor[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]`, indicating `r tolower(tiktok_summary$Interpretation[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))])`.

**Netflix:** The correlation analyses reveal that the self-reported addiction scores for Netflix are strongly correlated with most of the impulsivity measures. The strongest correlation is with `r netflix_summary$Variable[which.max(abs(netflix_summary$Correlation))]` (ρ = `r netflix_summary$Correlation[which.max(abs(tiktok_summary$Correlation))]`, 95% CI \[`r netflix_summary$CI_Lower[which.max(abs(netflix_summary$Correlation))]`, `r netflix_summary$CI_Upper[which.max(abs(netflix_summary$Correlation))]`\]), with a Bayes Factor of `r netflix_summary$Bayes_Factor[which.max(abs(netflix_summary$Correlation))]`, indicating `r tolower(netflix_summary$Interpretation[which.max(abs(netflix_summary$Correlation))])`.
